issues.legal_issue: An acquisition to establish an industrial complex serving broader economic interests is for a public purpose and is not colourable merely because private enterprises initiated or benefit from the project.
material_facts: The land was acquired for a planned diamond-processing complex intended to accommodate multiple industrial units, rather than solely one company.
The project formed part of the State’s industrial-development policy and was expected to promote exports, employment, and industrial growth.
Private companies initiated the proposal, entered into a memorandum with a state-owned corporation, and stood to benefit from allotments and supporting facilities.
The State remained interested in proceeding with the project even after one of the companies expressed unwillingness to proceed.
The Court found no material showing that the Government had forsaken public interest to serve private interests.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition served a public purpose and was not a colourable exercise of power; private initiative and incidental private benefit did not alter its public-purpose character.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 3(f), 4(1), and 6(1) and (3) of the Land Acquisition Act, a public-purpose declaration is conclusive subject to challenge for colourable exercise of power. Public purpose includes an object in which the general interest of the community is directly and vitally concerned. Industrial development by private enterprise may serve public purpose, although not every industry necessarily does. The Court relied on Hamabai Framjee Petit v. Secretary of State for India, Somawanti v. State of Punjab, Jage Ram v. State of Haryana, Bajirao T. Kate v. State of Maharashtra, and State of Punjab v. Gurdial Singh. A colourable exercise occurs when power is used to attain ends beyond its sanctioned purpose.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and planned_multi_unit_industrial_complex and broader_public_benefits_expected and government_commitment_independent_of_private_participant

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: Landholders challenged a government acquisition of land.
predicates.planned_multi_unit_industrial_complex: The government planned to use the acquired land for an industrial complex accommodating multiple enterprises.
predicates.broader_public_benefits_expected: The project was expected to promote broader economic interests such as industrial growth, exports, or employment.
predicates.government_commitment_independent_of_pri: The government remained committed to the project even when a private participant was unwilling to proceed.

issues.definition: When landholders challenge an acquisition planned for a multi-enterprise industrial complex with expected broader public benefits, and the government remains committed independently of a private participant, the acquisition serves public purpose and is not colourable.

issues.legal_issue: Compensation paid from the funds of a state-controlled corporation satisfies the public-funding requirement even when the funds originated in a private company’s advance payment credited to the corporation.
material_facts: A state-owned and controlled corporation paid a substantial amount towards compensation.
A private company had paid money to the corporation, and the evidence supported the finding that it was credited as advance lease premium under an arrangement with the corporation.
The corporation’s funds were used to pay compensation, and the State had indicated that it would provide funds if needed to meet the acquisition cost.
The Court found no sufficient basis to treat the private company’s payment as an advance compensation payment made directly for the acquisition.
issues.conclusion: The compensation payment from the corporation’s funds satisfied the requirement that compensation for a public-purpose acquisition be paid wholly or partly from public revenues or an eligible public fund.
issues.legal_principle: The second proviso to Section 6(1), read with Explanation 2, requires that compensation for a public-purpose acquisition be paid wholly or partly from public revenues or a qualifying fund; funds of a corporation owned or controlled by the State are treated as public revenues. The source from which a fund originated is not determinative once it has become the fund of the state-controlled corporation; its present ownership matters. The Court relied on Somawanti v. State of Punjab, Jage Ram v. State of Haryana, Manubhai Jehtalal Patel v. State of Gujarat, and Srinivasa Co-operative House Building Society Ltd. v. Madam G. Sastry.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: Landholders challenged an acquisition for which a public-purpose declaration was made.
predicates.compensation_paid_from_state_controlled_: A corporation owned or controlled by the State paid at least part of the compensation from funds held by that corporation.

issues.definition: When landholders challenge an acquisition and a state-controlled corporation pays compensation from its funds, the public-funding requirement is satisfied.

issues.legal_issue: A public-purpose description is not invalid for vagueness when it is understandable in context and the landholders understood the proposed acquisition well enough to make detailed objections without showing substantial prejudice.
material_facts: The notifications described the purpose as establishing a diamond park, and the responsible industrial-development officer was identified in the notification.
The industrial-policy context and the notices issued during the objection process made clear that the project concerned industrial development and diamond-processing units.
The landholders filed detailed objections addressing the acquisition’s purposes and circumstances.
The landholders did not demonstrate that the wording prevented them from effectively objecting or otherwise caused substantial prejudice.
issues.conclusion: The stated public purpose was not so vague as to invalidate the notification or the subsequent proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4(1) and 5A require sufficient specification of the public purpose to enable meaningful objections, assessed in light of the facts and circumstances of the case. A court should not invalidate acquisition proceedings for a theoretical ambiguity without a real and substantial grievance or prejudice. The Court relied on Aflatoon v. Lt. Governor of Delhi, Madhya Pradesh Housing Board v. Md. Shafi, and Munshi Singh v. Union of India.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: Landholders challenged a government acquisition on the ground that its stated purpose was vague.
predicates.purpose_description_understandable_in_co: The stated purpose conveyed its nature when read in the context of the project and the information accompanying the acquisition process.
predicates.objectors_understood_purpose_and_made_de: The landholders understood the proposed use of the land and submitted detailed objections about it.
predicates.no_substantial_prejudice_shown: The landholders did not show that the wording prevented meaningful objections or caused substantial prejudice.

issues.definition: When landholders challenge an acquisition for vagueness, but the stated purpose is understandable in context, they understood it and made detailed objections, and they show no substantial prejudice, the notification is not invalid for vagueness.

issues.legal_issue: Environmental and security objections do not invalidate an industrial land acquisition when the proposed activity presents no material pollution or security threat and the available evidence does not establish a countervailing public harm.
material_facts: The proposed diamond-cutting and polishing operations did not generate material emissions, noise, or effluents, apart from minimal impacts associated with habitation and transport.
Military and scientific authorities indicated that the project would not create security problems, and the defence ministry reported no direct national-security implications.
The landholders relied on environmental guidelines, but the record did not establish that the acquired land was prime agricultural land being used to grow crops.
The Court found no material showing that the project would harm public health, safety, or security so as to outweigh its public benefits.
issues.conclusion: The environmental and security objections did not justify invalidating the acquisition.
issues.legal_principle: Environmental and security concerns must be assessed realistically in light of the proposed activity, the characteristics of the site, the evidence, and the need to balance economic and environmental interests. Guidelines concerning sensitive areas and agricultural land must be considered on the available facts; unsupported concerns do not establish that a project is detrimental to public health, safety, or security.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: Landholders challenged an acquisition on environmental or security grounds.
predicates.proposed_activity_has_no_material_pollut: The proposed industrial activity does not create material pollution through emissions, noise, or effluent.
predicates.relevant_authorities_report_no_security_: Authorities responsible for relevant security interests reported no material security threat from the proposed project.
predicates.no_evidence_of_countervailing_environmen: The record does not establish environmental harm sufficient to outweigh the project’s public benefits.

issues.definition: When landholders raise environmental or security objections to an acquisition, but the proposed activity creates no material pollution, relevant authorities report no security threat, and no countervailing environmental harm is established, those objections do not invalidate the acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: A claim that an acquisition includes excessive land does not invalidate it without material evidence that the authorities failed to assess the land required for present and future needs.
material_facts: The landholders asserted that the acquired area exceeded reasonable requirements but provided no material supporting that assertion.
The State relied on a layout plan and an assessment of the area needed for industrial plots, a green belt, housing, common facilities, and other amenities.
The Court considered the extent of land required to be primarily within the State’s domain, while observing that a fresh assessment and exclusion of any land found excessive would be desirable.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition was not invalidated on the ground that excessive land had been acquired, although the State was advised to reassess the area and exclude any portion found to be unnecessary.
issues.legal_principle: The extent of land required for an acquisition is primarily for the State to determine in light of present and future needs. A challenge alleging excess must be supported by material showing that the assessment was improper; unsupported assertions do not warrant invalidation. The Court also observed that a reassessment and exclusion of land found excessive would be desirable.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: Landholders challenged a government acquisition as including more land than was required.
predicates.extent_assessed_for_present_and_future_n: The acquiring authority assessed the extent of land required in light of present and future project needs.
predicates.no_material_evidence_of_excess: The challengers provided no material evidence that the assessed extent exceeded what the project required.

issues.definition: When landholders challenge an acquisition as excessive, the extent was assessed for present and future needs, and no material evidence of excess is provided, the acquisition is not invalid for excess land.
